Days, months and years are different kinds of count

Start with a week on a calendar, then separate the repeating weekday cycle from the changing lengths of months.

By Biel Sardà · Published 1 Oct 2026 · Suggest a correction

Two counts on one page

A calendar date and a weekday answer different questions. “The 15th” tells you where you are within a month. “Tuesday” names a place in the repeating seven-day week. A month can begin on any weekday.

After Sunday comes Monday even when the month changes. The weekday cycle carries on; it does not restart at the beginning of each month.

Try it yourself

Move forward from an imaginary Monday. After seven days you arrive at another Monday. After eight, you reach Tuesday. The activity counts elapsed days, so the starting Monday is day zero.

This distinction matters when a question says “after three days”. Monday to Tuesday is one day, Tuesday to Wednesday is two, and Wednesday to Thursday is three. Counting the starting day as the first elapsed day would shift the answer.

A month is not four weeks

Four weeks contain 28 days. In the Gregorian calendar, months have 28, 29, 30 or 31 days. A 30-day month is four weeks plus two days; it is not an exact number of weeks.

An ordinary Gregorian year contains 365 days, and a leap year contains 366. The calendar arranges months to keep the year in step with the seasons. February supplies the extra day in a leap year.

Keep the units in view

“Two months” is not always the same number of elapsed days. January and February differ in length, and February can change in a leap year. When exact timing matters, use the actual dates instead of assuming every month has thirty days.

With days and years separated, we can next group years into centuries. The rule for a century is a counting convention; the leap-year rule solves a different problem.
